name: No Paying Customers
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Counting to Zero: The Uncomfortable Customer List
lesson.summary: Applying the previous chapter's evidentiary bar consistently across the industry reveals that the number of organizations paying quantum computing companies recurring money because quantum hardware outperforms classical alternatives on a task they need done is close to zero.
lesson.body:
Apply the evidentiary bar from the last chapter, real money changing hands, a recurring relationship, independent disclosure, consistently across superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, and neutral-atom quantum hardware companies, and a stark pattern emerges: essentially no independent, arm's-length customer today pays a quantum computing company on a recurring basis because that company's quantum computer demonstrably outperforms a classical computer, GPU cluster, or well-tuned classical heuristic on a task that matters to that customer's actual business. This is a strong claim, so it is worth being precise about what it does and does not mean.

It does not mean there is no paying activity at all in the industry. There plainly is: researchers and universities pay modest cloud access fees to experiment with quantum hardware, and governments pay substantial sums for contracted R&D work. Both of those are real payments for real value, research access and contracted engineering effort, but neither one is payment for a solved business problem, which is the specific thing a sustainable revenue model requires, as laid out earlier in this chapter. The distinction is not pedantic; a company can have millions of dollars flowing in from research contracts and cloud fees while still having zero customers of the kind that would let it eventually stand on its own without continued subsidy.

It is also worth being fair about why this is the current state of affairs, because the honest explanation is more about physics than about deception. Today's quantum processors are widely described using the term NISQ, noisy intermediate-scale quantum, meaning they operate without full error correction and accumulate errors quickly as computations grow longer or more complex. The algorithms with rigorously proven, decisive advantages over classical methods, Shor's algorithm for factoring being the best known example, generally require far more qubits, and far lower error rates, than any machine built to date provides. So the absence of paying production customers is broadly consistent with the technology genuinely being early rather than being evidence, on its own, of wrongdoing or incompetence.

A rough way to feel the gap: cloud-accessible quantum hardware from various providers has been available in some form since roughly 2016 through 2019, depending on the provider. In a typical maturing technology market, a handful of firms usually cross from pilot to repeat-purchase production contracts within a few years of general availability, once the underlying capability clears a usefulness threshold. That transition, at meaningful commercial scale, has not visibly happened for quantum hardware in that same window. This is an illustrative observation rather than a rigorously counted statistic, but the gap itself is informative about how far the technology still has to go.

The chapters that follow this one dig into why: a major reason paying customers have not materialized is that classical computing keeps improving too, and on many of the very problems quantum computing was expected to win, better classical algorithms and raw GPU power have kept the classical alternative both cheaper and, for now, just as capable.
